results.title: Data Mirroring - Definition & Detailed Explanation - Computer Storage ...
results.content: What are the Benefits of Data Mirroring? What are the Drawbacks of Data Mirroring? How is Data Mirroring Different from Data Replication? I. What is Data Mirroring? Data mirroring is a technique used in data storage and management to create and maintain an exact copy of data on a separate storage device or server. This process involves duplicating data in real-time, ensuring that any changes made to the original data are immediately reflected in the mirrored copy. Data mirroring is commonly used to increase data availability, improve fault tolerance, and enhance disaster recovery capabilities. How Does Data Mirroring Work? When data is written to the primary storage device, it is simultaneously copied to the mirrored storage device using a mirroring software or hardware solution. In synchronous mirroring, data is copied to the mirrored device in real-time, ensuring that both copies are always identical. In asynchronous mirroring, there may be a slight delay between when data is written to the primary device and when it is copied to the mirrored device, but the delay is typically minimal. What are the Benefits of Data Mirroring? Data mirroring offers several benefits, including: Improved data availability: By maintaining a mirrored copy of data, organizations can ensure that data remains accessible even in the event of hardware failures or other disruptions. Faster recovery times: In the event of a disaster or data corruption, organizations can quickly switch to the mirrored copy of data to minimize downtime and data loss. What are the Drawbacks of Data Mirroring? While data mirroring offers many benefits, there are also some drawbacks to consider, including: Cost: Maintaining a mirrored copy of data requires additional storage resources, which can increase costs for organizations. While data mirroring involves creating an exact copy of data in real-time, data replication involves copying data to a separate location for backup or disaster recovery purposes. Overall, data mirroring is a valuable tool for organizations looking to improve data availability, enhance fault tolerance, and streamline disaster recovery processes. By understanding the benefits, drawbacks, and common use cases of data mirroring, organizations can make informed decisions about implementing this technology in their data management strategies.

results.content: # iPhone Mirroring is currently a privacy and legal risk on work Macs. One of the new features of iOS 18 and macOS Sequoia is iPhone Mirroring – but using this with a personal iPhone on a work Mac currently creates a privacy risk for employees, and a legal risk for businesses. The problem, as cybersecurity company Sevco discovered, is that apps on the iPhone get treated as Mac apps, and that means their presence is included in corporate IT audits …. ## How iPhone Mirroring treats apps. Sevco found that when iPhone Mirroring is use, any iPhone app you run creates an entry in the Mac library here:. That is, the Mac treats them as if they were Mac apps. This means that when companies run automated network audits, to check that all the apps on their Macs are properly authorized and licensed, the iPhone apps will be identified. ## The privacy and legal risks. For iPhone users, that creates a potential privacy risk, because your employer will be able to see your iPhone apps. To be clear, they *can’t* see the data in them, but Sevco says even knowing which apps you use could have serious implications. > For iPhone users, this Apple bug is a major privacy risk because it can expose aspects of their personal lives that they don’t want to share or that could put them at risk. > For companies, this bug represents a new data liability from potentially collecting private employee data. If this bug is not addressed, it may lead to violation of major privacy laws such as CCPA, potential litigation, and federal agency enforcement. ## Apple is working on a fix; disclosure couldn’t wait. *Image: 9to5Mac collage of images from Apple and J Lee on Unsplash*.
